title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
extended_summary:
This paper reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in educational settings, with a particular focus on what data are collected from teachers, what roles teachers play in AI-based research, what benefits AI offers, and what challenges teachers face. The authors searched Web of Science for English-language journal articles published over the previous 20 years and identified 44 studies that met their inclusion criteria. The review was motivated by the observation that AI in education has advanced faster than teachers’ pedagogical integration of it, and that teachers’ perspectives have been underrepresented in prior literature.

Across the reviewed studies, the most common teacher-related data were self-reports and grading data, with additional use of observation, video, interviews, feedback/discourse, log data, eye tracking, and audiovisual/accelerometry. Teachers were found to serve several roles in AI development and use: as models for training AI systems, as sources of data on professional development and student behavior, as validators of automated assessment, and as providers of pedagogical guidance. The review also found that AI can support teachers in planning, implementation, and assessment, especially by improving monitoring, feedback, intervention, and automated scoring.

At the same time, the authors identify important challenges, including limited reliability and technical capacity of AI systems, context dependence, limited infrastructure, and limited teacher knowledge. They conclude that AI currently tends to reduce workload and support instructional decision-making, but that broader teacher involvement, more multimodal data, and more attention to pre-service teacher education are needed to make AI systems more pedagogically useful and robust across settings.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and does not provide pooled effect estimates. The evidence base summarized is largely qualitative/correlational and heterogeneous across settings and AI methods.
impact_tier_rationale: The review suggests practical benefits for teacher workflow and classroom monitoring, but it reports no pooled impact sizes and highlights important implementation failures and reliability limits. Overall impact appears promising but unclear rather than clearly moderate or large.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review does not estimate a single effect size, but it synthesizes 44 empirical studies on teachers' AI use and finds consistent operational benefits alongside clear constraints. The main benefits were planning support, timely monitoring, immediate feedback, reduced teacher workload, and automated assessment/scoring; however, the review also highlights reliability, technical capacity, infrastructure, and usability problems that limit real-world efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative synthesis of reported teacher workload, monitoring, feedback, planning, and assessment functions across 44 studies

finding.finding_summary: The review covers AI-supported instruction and assessment across multiple subjects, with the strongest emphasis on supporting teaching practice rather than direct student achievement. It reports that AI can help teachers adapt content, monitor learning, and automate scoring, but also notes that many systems are context-dependent and sometimes fail to assess complex or multimodal student work accurately.
finding.measure: Reported instructional/assessment uses across subject domains (e.g., English readability, ICT literacy, mathematics, science/STEM)

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, AI was sometimes used to track engagement, concentration, and teacher/student interaction, suggesting potential benefits for monitoring participation and affective states. At the same time, the review notes that some systems were slow, uninteresting, or insufficiently adaptive, which can reduce teacher enthusiasm and limit sustained use.
finding.measure: Engagement, concentration, interaction, and teacher-reported interest/usability across reviewed studies
